title: Losar again

cards: A guest steps into a Tibetan home on new year's morning, and before anything else, someone holds out a wooden box, split in two.

One side is heaped with roasted barley flour, the other with barley grain, stalks of grain standing up like little flags. The guest tosses a pinch into the air, then another, then a third, and puts a pinch on the tongue.
Then the greetings begin. This is Losar. You met its brooms and prayer flags back on day six ninety-three.
Today, look at it with this year's Tibetan map in hand.

teach.b: In the Tibetan block, you met a way Tibetan teachers describe their path: three vehicles practiced together, not one after another. Renunciation, compassion, and the diamond path.
Losar isn't a teaching on that map, but it can be walked through with one.

First, letting go. In the last days of the old year, houses are scrubbed, and old dust and old troubles are carried out the door. That's the household version of renunciation: the old year is over, so you stop holding it.
Second, sharing. The pinch of barley isn't kept. It's thrown up and out, an offering, before anyone eats.
Then come the visits, the gifts, and the greeting tashi delek, wishing good fortune on whoever you meet. The fresh year starts by giving something away. Third, the diamond path.
In the monasteries, the turn of the year brings rituals and chanting, and in some places masked dances.
And in the first month, by tradition, comes the Great Prayer festival, Monlam Chenmo, which Tibetan histories say Tsongkhapa, founder of the Gelug school, began in Lhasa.
Monks gather to pray for the world, and lay people come to offer lamps and food. Monlam means an aspiration prayer: a wish set out ahead of you. So the year begins with all three at once.
Clear the corner. Throw the pinch. Set out the wish.
None waits for the others to be finished, which is just what those teachers said about the vehicles.

how: Tibetans and Himalayan Buddhist communities keep Losar by the lunar calendar with house cleaning, new prayer flags, family visits, offerings of barley flour and grain, and monastery rituals; in the first month, monasteries in some places also hold Monlam prayer gatherings.

games.q: it's new year's morning in a Tibetan home, and you're handed a box of barley flour and grain. what do you do?
o: take a pinch, toss it up, then taste a little.
games.why: the pinch goes up into the air first, as an offering, and only then onto the tongue.

practice: Picture one corner of your home, a shelf, a drawer, a spot by the door, and with a few breaths, see what's there from a year that's already over and decide what goes.

With the next few breaths, think of one person who might use something you'd let go of. With the last few, set out one wish for the coming year, short and plain, as if you were writing it on a flag for the wind.

wordCard.voice: Losar. The Tibetan new year: houses cleaned, offerings shared, and in the monasteries, rituals and the Great Prayer. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan smon lam: an aspiration prayer; the Great Prayer festival is Monlam Chenmo.

carryVoice: Your line: a fresh year. Letting go, sharing and a wish, all at once. See you tomorrow.
